info.title: browser-box
info.description: One self-hosted Chromium (Steel) with its tools behind one door. The same tools are served over MCP at /mcp. The calling agent is the brain; the box executes.

post.summary: Plain HTTP GET of a public URL, no browser
post.description:
Plain HTTP GET, no browser. Fastest and free. Use it FIRST for any page that is server-rendered HTML, JSON or plain text — news sites, docs, APIs, RSS.
Do NOT use when: the page needs JavaScript to render, is behind a login, or blocks bots.
Returns: text (HTML stripped to readable text), status_code, final_url.

post.summary: Open a URL in the real browser and return its text, links and optionally a screenshot
post.description:
Open a URL in the real browser and return its rendered text, links and optionally a screenshot. Use when fetch returned nothing useful because the page renders with JavaScript.
Do NOT use when: fetch already answered (this costs a browser slot), or the task needs clicking and typing rather than reading.
One browser runs at a time on this host; this call waits for the lane and then holds it.
The screenshot is a SECOND, independent page load, so on a page that changes between loads the picture and the text may not agree, and that navigation is NOT pre-flighted. Ask for it when the picture is the evidence.
Returns: text, title, links, status_code, and screenshot_base64 (JPEG) when asked for.

post.summary: Create, list or release a persistent browser session (logins survive between calls)
post.description:
Create, list or release a persistent browser session. A session keeps cookies and a profile across calls, which is how logged-in work is done.
create -> returns session_id and the live view URL so a human can sign in once.
list   -> what is currently open. release -> closes it and frees the lane.
Creating or releasing a session restarts the browser: act's tab starts again at about:blank.
Do NOT create a session for one-off public reads; `read` is cheaper and releases itself.

post.summary: Drive the browser in plain-words steps; Jev picks each element
post.description:
Drive the browser step by step in plain words: "open https://…", "click the Pricing link", "type 'running shoes' into the search box and press enter", "scroll down", "go back". You plan the steps; Jev, a decision model that never writes text, picks which element on the page each step means (typically ~0.3 s; page loads take longer). Up to 4 steps joined by "then" or "and" run in order.
When Jev is unsure it asks instead of guessing: status needs_clarification with options — answer with act(pick=<option pick>). Anything that looks hard to undo (buy, delete, send, post) comes back as needs_confirmation — answer with act(confirm=true) or act(confirm=false). Nothing risky runs unconfirmed.
Prefer act over task whenever you can say the steps: measured on search, forms, pagination, state and a JS app, it was 10–60x faster and as or more accurate on all but search (see the README). Read each step's did: a click on a link marked (page does not exist) is a wrong pick, so say which one you meant.
Use for clicking, typing, forms and multi-page flows. Do NOT use just to read a public page: fetch or read is cheaper. The tab stays where you left it between calls; creating or releasing a session restarts the browser and the tab starts again at about:blank.
Private and internal addresses are refused inside the browser itself, on every request and redirect.
Returns: status (done | failed | needs_clarification | needs_confirmation), steps (what ran and how each went), url, title, and the page's text when read_page=true.

post.summary: Drive an Orgo cloud desktop: screenshot, click, type, key, scroll, bash, start, stop
post.description:
Drive an Orgo cloud computer: a full Linux desktop with a browser and a shell, running OFF this box. You are the eyes — take a screenshot, decide, act, screenshot again. Coordinates are pixels in the most recent screenshot.
Actions: screenshot | click(x, y[, button, double]) | type(text) | key(key, e.g. "Return", "ctrl+c") | scroll(x, y[, direction, amount]) | bash(command) | start | stop.
Do NOT use for a web page that fetch or read can answer: this is a whole computer, billed per hour.
bash is a real shell on that computer, inside your Orgo account.
A computer bills until it is stopped. Call action=stop when you are finished.

post.summary: Hand a whole goal to an agent (Browser-Use in the browser, or Orgo on a desktop)
post.description:
Hand a whole goal to an agent and wait for its answer. Use it when you would rather not plan the steps yourself; you lose sight of each step, and every step costs model time.
Measured against act: 30–130 s per job, and less reliable. It failed a two-URL cookie job 2 of 3 times and a JS to-do app 3 of 3. Check its answer before trusting it.
surface="browser": Browser-Use works the goal in this box's browser, with a model choosing each step (one model call per step; a few steps take ~10-40 s). It gets a tab of its own and never touches act's tab. Private and internal addresses are refused inside the browser. Its tab is closed when it finishes: to look at the last page again, read final_url. Returns status (done | failed | incomplete | timed_out | cancelled | stopped), answer, steps, urls, final_url, tokens and estimated_cost_usd.
It holds the browser until it finishes, even if you stop waiting: this endpoint cannot hear a client give up. task(cancel=true) stops it, and the stopped task still reports what it did.
surface="computer": Orgo's hosted computer-use agent (Claude) works an Orgo desktop until the goal is done. Orgo ignores max_steps and caps its loop at 250 steps; timeout_seconds is the real bound, and hitting it aborts the run.
Do NOT use when one fetch or read answers it, or when you can drive the steps yourself with act or computer: that is faster, cheaper and you see every step.
